passage: At the flat's play area in Lucknow, Jahnavi held up her hand with two fingers crossed and whispered to Rafiq, "If I cross fingers, it's for luck. Do it too!" Rafiq crossed his, and the two waited beside the sandpit for the ice-cream van. When it rang its bell, they hugged. Next day Jahnavi made a different sign, a thumb tucked behind a fist. "That's our secret sign," she said. "It means come to the swing." Rafiq grinned and tucked his thumb too.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do with her fingers to bring luck?
qa.a: She crossed two fingers.

qa.q: What is Rafiq probably feeling when he copies the signs?
qa.a: He likely feels included and excited to share a secret with Jahnavi, since he grinned and copied at once. He might also just enjoy copying.

qa.q: What could an adult do when children invent secret signs?
qa.a: They can enjoy the game and remember it's playful, while reminding children to tell them about anything that makes them uneasy.

qa.q: How might another child who doesn't know the signs feel?
qa.a: They might feel left out or puzzled, since the secret signs only work for those who share them.

grounding: Crossed fingers and secret signs are playful conventions that only work within a shared group.

passage:
"Promise you won't tell," said Farhan, holding up crossed fingers behind his back.
"What's that?" asked Ganga.
"It's a promise sign. Kids at my old school did it."
"We do a pinky."
"That's different!"
"It's the same," said Ganga. "It just looks different."
They grinned. "Okay," said Farhan, and showed his pinky too. "Ready? Let's hide the ball and see if Papa finds it."

qa.q: What sign did Farhan hold up behind his back?
qa.a: He held up crossed fingers behind his back.

qa.q: What does Ganga seem to think about the different signs?
qa.a: Ganga thinks they mean the same promise even though they look different, and the grin shows Ganga is happy about it. Farhan may feel unsure at first because his sign is the one he knows.

qa.q: What would help children who use different signs?
qa.a: They can explain their signs and choose one for the game together, as Farhan and Ganga did.

qa.q: How might Farhan see the pinky compared with his crossed fingers?
qa.a: He might find it new and interesting, showing that groups have their own signs.

grounding: Crossed fingers and pinky promises are playful conventions that vary by group.

passage:
Note by Vidya, KG teacher. Sports day lucky draw.
While we pulled names for the class prize, Preeti sat with both hands crossed, fingers twisted round each other, eyes squeezed shut. When her name wasn't called, she uncrossed them, looked at her fingers and said, “They didn't work.” Her friend showed her their group's secret sign: two taps on the nose, meaning “next time.” Preeti tapped her nose back and grinned. I noticed each little group has its own signs, and they love sharing them. 😊

qa.q: What was the secret sign Preeti's friend showed her?
qa.a: Two taps on the nose, meaning “next time.”

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she said, “They didn't work”?
qa.a: She felt disappointed that her crossed fingers didn't bring luck. She may also have felt a bit puzzled, since she believed in them.

qa.q: How could Vidya use what the note describes about the class's secret signs?
qa.a: Vidya could let the groups teach their signs to each other in a circle time, so the fun is shared and nobody feels left out.

qa.q: How might Preeti's friend see the nose-tap?
qa.a: The friend saw it as a kind way to cheer Preeti up and include her in their shared sign.

grounding: The note shows a preschooler crossing her fingers for luck and enjoying a group's playful secret sign.

passage: At the village school playground, Sunaina hooked her little finger round Disha's. “Pinky promise you'll save me a swing.” Disha looked puzzled and crossed two fingers instead. “In our lane we do this.” “Crossed fingers are for luck!” said Sunaina. “Not in my lane,” Disha giggled. “Crossed means promise.” They tried each other's signs, laughing. In the end they did both, pinkies hooked and fingers crossed, and ran to the swings, which Disha had saved.

qa.q: What does crossed fingers mean in Disha's lane?
qa.a: Promise.

qa.q: What were the girls feeling as they tried each other's signs?
qa.a: They felt amused and playful, enjoying the mix-up. At first Sunaina was a little puzzled that Disha used a different sign.

qa.q: What does this scene show about how to handle different signs?
qa.a: Trying each other's signs and laughing about it works better than insisting only one meaning is right.

qa.q: How might a child from a third lane see their double promise?
qa.a: They might find it confusing or funny, and have their own sign to add, since these signs vary by group.

grounding: Two children find that crossed fingers and pinky promises mean different things in different groups, and enjoy sharing them.

passage: In the kindergarten yard in Melbourne, Bao ran up to Noa and tapped his ear twice. Noa tapped her ear back. That was their secret sign: meet at the sandpit. Before the egg-and-spoon race, Noa crossed her fingers tight behind her back. “For luck,” she whispered. Bao crossed his too, though he wasn't racing. When Noa's egg stayed on the spoon all the way, they both waved crossed fingers in the air and ran to the sandpit together.

qa.q: What did two taps on the ear mean for Bao and Noa?
qa.a: Meet at the sandpit.

qa.q: Why did Bao cross his fingers even though he wasn't racing?
qa.a: He wanted Noa to do well and felt excited and loyal to his friend, sharing her hope for luck.

qa.q: What would you advise a teacher who notices this secret sign?
qa.a: Enjoy it and leave it as their playful thing, while making sure other children are not left out of games.

qa.q: What would change if another child didn't know the ear-tap sign?
qa.a: That child might feel left out or confused, because such signs only work for those who share them.

grounding: Two preschoolers use crossed fingers for luck and a shared secret sign for play.

passage:
Sports day at the school, and the lemon-and-spoon race was next. Pooja stood at the line with both hands behind her back, fingers crossed so hard they hurt.

"Why are your fingers like that?" asked a boy beside her.

"For luck," Pooja said.

Across the field, Damini tugged her own left ear twice. Pooja grinned and tugged hers back. It was their secret sign: meet at the swings after.

Pooja's lemon fell halfway. She laughed, picked it up and walked the rest.

qa.q: What was their secret sign?
qa.a: Tugging the left ear twice, which meant meet at the swings after.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling as she crossed her fingers so hard they hurt?
qa.a: She was likely nervous and hopeful about the race. The grin when Damini tugged her ear shows she also felt happy and close to her friend.

qa.q: What makes the secret sign work between Pooja and Damini?
qa.a: They both know what the ear tug means, so it is a private, playful message that others around them would not understand.

qa.q: How does the boy beside Pooja see her crossed fingers?
qa.a: He doesn't know the custom and is curious, so he asks why her fingers look like that.

grounding: It shows a child crossing her fingers for luck and sharing a secret ear-tug sign that only her friend understands.
